name: Chloe Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I process pension credit claims for older people at the small benefits office in Westfield, next to the library. Most of the day I'm checking bank statements, working out entitlement and phoning people who've filled in the wrong box. A lot of my claimants are in their eighties, so the calls take ages and I don't mind that at all. What wears me out is the new rules every April, because I have to relearn half the calculation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you feel about the AI tools some offices use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I don't use them. They put a chat box on our system last year and I closed it the first day and haven't opened it since. I like knowing how I got to a number. My boyfriend Ravi is an electrician, and he's the same with gadgets, which is probably why we get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, sensible, now we can stop talking about it. At work I'd tell people we wasted a year of meetings on that chat box. I don't post online much, so I'd leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. My job stays, the pay's good, and there are three other benefits offices within a bus ride if I ever want to move. Nothing in that picture touches me much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd keep saving about 500 a month, and Ravi and I would buy a house in the next two years like we planned. I'd go for the April rules training, same as every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the fuss died down and the office went quiet again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The April rule changes, always. Every year somebody's pension credit gets worked out wrong because the guidance came late, and that's a people problem, not an AI one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ravi say about AI being hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi (my boyfriend) would say he told me so, because he says that about most things. He'd also say his van's satnav is the only clever machine he trusts.

say: I'd say it's **sensible** and we can finally stop talking about it.
I'd tell colleagues we wasted a **year of meetings** on that chat box.
think: My **job and pay** stay, with three other offices within a bus ride.
Nothing in this picture **touches me** much, so I'm relieved.
do: Carry on with **pension credit** claims exactly as now.
Keep saving about **500 a month** toward a house with Ravi.
Attend the **April rules** training as usual.
feel: **Calm**, like the fuss died down and the office went quiet.
S0.quote: Every year somebody's pension credit gets worked out wrong because the guidance came late, and that's a people problem, not an AI one.
fieldNote: Chloe is **settled** and sees nothing new to fear here.
Her real irritation is the yearly **rule changes**.
She enjoys the slow calls with **older claimants**.

steps.text: Keep processing pension credit claims without the chat box
Save about 500 a month toward a house with Ravi

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be careful, especially with older claimants who can't use apps. At work I'd keep my head down and do what I'm told. I wouldn't get involved in anything loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd come for my bit first. Entitlement calculations, letters and phone questions are exactly the kind of tasks on that card. I'm not quick with new systems, so if they cut the team I'd be near the front of the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my savings untouched and hold off on the house for a year. I'd do the new system training because I'd have to, but nothing extra. I'd also look at jobs where you deal with people face to face, maybe the council's home visiting team for older residents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It sits in my chest when I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off on the house. How would Ravi take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd grumble, because he's been looking at listings every Sunday. But he'd understand, because it's my income that's the shaky one, not his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently from colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of them would learn the tools fast and try to stay. I'd rather move to a job with home visits than spend my days arguing with a screen.

Do only the **required training** on the new system.
Apply to the council's **home visiting team** for older residents.
feel: **Anxious**, a tightness in the chest when she thinks about it.
S1.quote: I'd rather move to a job with home visits than spend my days arguing with a screen.
fieldNote: She expects to be **cut early** because she avoids new tools.
Her instinct is to **move**, not to adapt in place.
Ravi's **steady trade** gives the household some security.

steps.text: Put the house purchase on hold for a year
Apply to the council home visiting team for older residents
Leave the savings untouched as a fallback

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and somebody should have stopped it. At work I'd say the government didn't think about the old people who can't use any of this. I still wouldn't post, but I'd say it to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm out of a job by 2028. My work is all sums and letters and phone calls, so I don't get the three extra years that Ravi does. I'd be 29 with no job and a skill nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house hunt straight away and keep the savings for rent. I'd ask Ravi whether I could train as an electrician's mate with him, because hands-on work buys until about 2031. I'd sign up for any government help going, because that's what it's there for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't worry, I've got savings and Ravi's working. Then I'd go home and cry, probably. My mum would bring round a curry and pretend it was nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really work with Ravi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try. Ravi (my boyfriend) says I'd be terrible as an electrician's mate, but three years of wages is three years.

say: I'd call it **madness** that somebody should have stopped.
I'd say the government forgot **older people** who can't use any of this.
think: I'm **out of a job** by 2028 with no three-year buffer.
At **29** I'd have a skill nobody needs.
do: Stop the **house hunt** at once and keep savings for rent.
Train as an **electrician's mate** with Ravi for the robot gap.
Sign up for any **government help** on offer.
S2.quote: Ravi (my boyfriend) says I'd be terrible as an electrician's mate, but three years of wages is three years.
fieldNote: She is plain about expecting **job loss** with no buffer.
The robot gap makes Ravi's **trade** her lifeboat.
She hides fear from **family** while feeling it strongly.

steps.text: Stop the house hunt and keep savings for rent
Train as an electrician's mate alongside Ravi
Apply for government jobseeker support and retraining grants

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the fast one, I'd say it should be stopped or slowed. At work I'd say we need a proper plan for staff. I'd still keep it to work and family, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the same ending with more warning. My job goes around 2031, but I'd have time to train properly in something hands-on. That gives me until about 2034, which feels like a real gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a proper electrical installation course part-time in the first year, not just being Ravi's helper. I'd keep my job while I study, because the pay is good. We might still buy a small house, since Ravi's job is safer for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick about it. Like I had time to pack before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of training would scare you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The maths and the exams, funnily enough, though I do sums all day. It's being the oldest person in a class full of eighteen-year-olds that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still avoid the AI tools during those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, unless they made it part of the job. I'd rather put my effort into learning wiring than learning a chat box that's going to replace me anyway.

say: I'd say it should be **slowed** and staff need a **proper plan**.
I'd keep my views to **work and family**, not online.
think: My job still ends around **2031**, just with more warning.
Proper **hands-on training** would buy me until about 2034.
do: Start a part-time **electrical installation** course in the first year.
Keep the **pension credit** job and its pay while studying.
Consider a **small house** with Ravi, since his job lasts longer.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, like having time to **pack** before moving.
S3.quote: I'd rather put my effort into learning wiring than learning a chat box that's going to replace me anyway.
fieldNote: Five years turns her into a **trainee** rather than a helper.
She refuses AI tools because she sees them as her **replacement**.
Her main fear is **social**, being older than classmates.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time electrical installation course
Keep the pension credit job while studying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change, so let's not panic. At work I'd tell people to keep doing their jobs well. I'd be the calm one in the office, at least on the outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, because it ends the same way. I'd be 37 when my job goes. I'd probably leave training until year five or six, which might be a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house with Ravi in the next two years and keep saving. I'd stay in pension credit claims as long as they'd have me. Around 2031 I'd start an electrical course, or maybe something like care work with older people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious underneath, calm on top. Ten years makes AGI feel far away, which I know is a trick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said leaving it late might be a mistake. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm like that. I don't move until I have to, and I've never regretted staying put. I might this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would push you to start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the first colleague get let go, probably. If Margaret on the next desk went, I'd sign up for a course that week.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without doubt, because I'd have no time to train and I'm slow to change. What would help is paid training for hands-on trades and a bit of money to get through it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the old people. Half my claimants can't work a phone, and nobody in any of these pictures is thinking about who they'll talk to.

headlineQuote: Half my claimants can't work a phone, and nobody in any of these pictures is thinking about who they'll talk to.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old** pension credit caseworker who refuses to use the office's AI chat box.
She feels **secure** if AI is hype, and expects to be cut early under real change.
Her escape route is **hands-on work**, often alongside her electrician boyfriend Ravi.
She tends to **wait** until she must move, and knows it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time to train and is slow to change.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** in hands-on trades and money to live on while training.
